comments.text: Beautiful documentary. I'm curious about the population genetics of the Faroe Islands. Given the islands' long history of relative isolation and the documented founder effect, how do people traditionally navigate family relationships when choosing partners? Is awareness of shared ancestry part of everyday life, and has immigration changed this over recent generations? I'd be especially interested in hearing from Faroese residents.

replies.author: @mindhunterspirithunter1374
replies.text: @HappyTravel99 Thank you for your response, I am a documentary maker myself,  my question is based on curiosity and respect.  I learn from other doccie makers.  thank you.  I have researched the answer.

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text:
Thank you for such a thoughtful and fascinating question! ❤️ The Faroe Islands' long history of relative isolation certainly makes their population genetics and family ancestry an interesting subject. In small communities, family connections and knowledge of ancestry can be particularly meaningful, but we wouldn't want to make assumptions about how Faroese people choose their partners or how these traditions have changed over time.
We're especially curious to hear from Faroese residents too! If anyone from the islands is reading this, we'd love to know: How aware are people of their extended family connections today, and has immigration changed that over the generations? Your firsthand experiences would add so much to this conversation. 😊

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: It's fascinating, isn't it? 😊 The Faroe Islands have very few naturally growing trees because of their strong winds, cool climate, and relatively thin soils. Trees can grow in sheltered areas, though, and some have been planted around villages and gardens. That's why the islands are mostly covered in beautiful green grass rather than forests! 🌿❤️

Yet, the country itself is amazing (and I learned from friends that visited it, the people are super kind + you have a national treasure with Eivor … I watched her live on stage and it was mindblowingly great) has been on my wishlist but there are other ways to make an income besides these fish pens

comments.text: A little bit or research please! There are trees growing up to 80 feet high. There is evidence of woodlands of birch before human occupation. Although winds and salt are a problem, the biggest problem when it comes for woodlands is the sheep! Despite that, go to Viðarlundin Park, and it is full of birch, tall spruce trees, and even some more exoctic varieties. There is no reason more trees cannot be grown. There are 27 plantations already, most small, community run affairs.

comments.text:
Small world...

The building on the right at 5:09 is Mikkeller pub. I went in there for beer and noticed that the graphics on the beer labels were identical to (a now closed) Mikkeller bar in Los Angeles that I used to drink at. As it turns out, as I understand it, the owners of the two pubs went to college together in Los Angeles. The Faroe Islands is world's away from Los Angeles. Having the two bars be related seemed crazy at the time. Anyway, good times...

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: What an amazing connection! 😊 It really is a small world, especially when a place as far away as the Faroe Islands has a surprising link to Los Angeles. Thank you for sharing this personal memory—it adds such a wonderful story to that little scene at 5:09. We love hearing these unexpected connections from our viewers! comments.author: @thessalonikatbenny6948
comments.text: I would love to come and see what is there... but I'm 70.  Are there hospitals?  Do people speak much English?  Are there places where elders can volunteer to give our lives meaning?  That is what I'm looking for - a place to contribute to, not just look at.  Are there places for us to live?  If all housing is passed through families, what would a new person do for a living space?  I've volunteered with zoos, pet rescue organizations, and schools.  I cannot lift heavy objects, but having lived in 10 countries already, I like to think I get along with most everyone.  Would the Faroe Islands accept me?

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text:
Thank you for sharing such a thoughtful and heartfelt comment. At 70, your experience and desire to contribute could be a wonderful asset to a small community like the Faroe Islands. English is widely spoken there, so communication is generally quite easy for visitors. The islands also have hospitals and healthcare services, with the National Hospital located in Tórshavn.

There are volunteer opportunities as well. For example, the official “Closed for Maintenance” programme welcomes volunteers aged 18+ and uses English for communication, although some projects can require physical activity.

Finding a permanent home would be a more complicated question, and residency rules depend on your nationality. For most non-Nordic citizens, a work and residence permit is required to live and work in the Faroe Islands.

But as for whether someone with your experience, kindness, and willingness to help could find a place in the community—we certainly hope so. Your story sounds like it could be the beginning of a very meaningful new chapter. Thank you for watching, and we hope you get the opportunity to visit someday! ❤️
